title: Field sketching and nature journaling habit
summary: Learn to draw living things straight from observation, in short sessions outdoors or at a window, using a pen and a cheap sketchbook. The goal is a looking habit and a growing stock of shapes, poses and notes you can raid later when you invent things.
learning_outcomes: Fill a page with quick studies of one living subject in about 20 minutes
Pair each sketch with a short written note (what, where, when, what it was doing)
Place the main mass of a subject before adding any detail
Keep a weekly sketching routine that survives a busy schedule

resources.title: John Muir Laws: nature journaling hub (free curriculum, video series, podcast)
resources.free_notes: Home page labels a Free Nature Journaling Curriculum, Free Online Lessons (workshop archive) and a free poster set. Priced or likely paid items listed there: Stanford Songbird Drawing Masterclass (dated 22 Oct to 19 Nov 2026), the online educator certification, the Naturalist Store. Cost of Nature Journal Club and the video series is not stated.
resources.notes: Start with the Free Nature Journaling Curriculum and the Nature Journal Connection video series listed on the home page, then follow his YouTube channel (youtube.com/user/JohnMuirLaws). Do the curriculum's early sessions before touching any subject-specific lesson.

resources.title: Urban Sketchers official YouTube channel
resources.free_notes: Public YouTube channel with workshop, symposium and sketchcrawl videos. I could not see a playlist list.
resources.notes: Pick two or three on-location workshop or sketchcrawl videos and copy the routine (what he draws first, how long per page), not the style. Good for urban rather than wild subjects.

resources.title: Botanical Art and Artists: Botanical Sketching and Sketchbooks
resources.free_notes: Linked from the site index; I opened a sister page on the same site (trees and leaves) and found no paywall, but this page itself was not opened. The site also sells courses and e-booklets.
resources.notes: Read for sketchbook set-up and how plant studies are laid out on a page. Page contents not opened by me; verify before relying on it.

resources.title: Cornell Lab Bird Academy: Nature Journaling and Field Sketching (plus free webinars)
resources.provider: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Bird Academy
resources.free_notes: Nature Journaling and Field Sketching and How to Paint Birds with Jane Kim were each listed at 99.99 USD in Oct 2026. Some webinars on the same site are free (for example a live sketching session with Liz Clayton Fuller). Use as supplementary only.
resources.notes: Paid course, so optional. If you want a structured outdoor-sketching course later, this is the one to price up; the free webinars on the same site are a cheaper taste.

practice.title: Window sketches
practice.description: Draw whatever living thing you can see outside a window (bird, tree, insect, cloud) with a pen, no pencil guidelines, one subject per page.

practice.title: One object, six angles
practice.description: Choose a leaf, feather or shell and draw it from six angles on one page, aiming for variety rather than neatness.

practice.title: Sketch plus three notes
practice.description: After each sketch, write three observations that a photo would not tell you, such as behaviour, texture or colour.

practice.title: Sixty-second gestures
practice.description: Draw birds or other moving animals in one-minute bursts, from live observation or a nature cam, to train fast placement.

practice.title: Local outing
practice.description: Spend a single outing at a nearby park, creek or botanic garden and fill two pages with whatever catches your eye.

done_when: You have at least eight dated sketchbook pages covering several different subjects
You can begin a sketch by placing the big mass, without pencil guidelines
You can stay on one subject for 20 minutes without drifting to something easier
Your pages include written observations, not only outlines
common_mistakes: Trying to make every page a finished showpiece, which kills the habit
Drawing only from photos, so the eye never trains on moving or changing subjects
Carrying too much kit, so setup becomes the reason not to start

school_reference.institution: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Bird Academy
school_reference.note: Sells a Nature Journaling and Field Sketching course (99.99 USD listed Oct 2026). Syllabus not read; reference for how a formal field-sketching course is packaged.

title: Plants, flowers and trees: construction, leaf and branch structure, growth patterns
summary: Treat plants as arrangements of simple forms: stems as bending tubes, leaves as curved flat planes, flower heads as bowls, discs or clusters. You learn how leaves attach, how branches fork, and which growth patterns repeat, so invented plants still look like they could grow.
learning_outcomes: Draw a leaf as a bent plane, including foreshortened and curling leaves
Show how a stem, node and leaf attach, including the thickness change at forks
Recognise and draw alternate, opposite, whorled and rosette leaf arrangements
Break a flower into a simple form and layer petals around it
Invent a believable plant by reusing real growth rules

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Plants (paper-model series plus workshops)
resources.free_notes: Page metadata describes these as free online tutorials and no paywall appeared. The downloadable flower and leaf model set links to a store-style /product/ page whose price I could not see; the site also sells books and runs paid classes.
resources.notes: Watch the eight-part paper-model series in order: Introduction, Symmetry, Foreshortening 1 and 2, Leaves and petals, Curling leaves 1 and 2, Conclusion. Then 'Flowers in Perspective' and 'Let's Draw Trees'. Fold the paper models yourself as he does.

resources.title: Drawabox Lesson 3: Applying Construction to Plants
resources.free_notes: Drawabox's server returned a bot-check page to my fetch, so I could not read the lesson or any price. The lesson title is confirmed from public community submission titles, and the /lesson/N URL pattern is confirmed by lesson 7 appearing in search results. Whether instructor critique sits behind a paid or supporter tier is not verified.
resources.notes: Do this after the paper-model series if you want a more rigid construction method (forms first, contour lines, then leaf detail). Expect a long homework set; read the lesson text on drawabox.com in a normal browser.

resources.title: Botanical Art and Artists: tips on drawing trees and leaves, plus sketchbook and pencil video tips
resources.free_notes: Page opened: a hub on leaf shape, veination and arrangement (phyllotaxis), leaf colour and watercolour technique, plus bark, twigs and buds and how to observe and plan tree drawings. Site describes itself as free to the reader and earns Amazon affiliate commission on book links. The same site also sells online courses and diplomas.
resources.notes: Read the trees-and-leaves hub for leaf shape, veination and leaf arrangement (phyllotaxis), plus bark, twigs and buds, then watch the pencil and leaf video tips linked from the same site (those linked pages not opened by me).

resources.title: Biodiversity Heritage Library: open-access natural history books and plates
resources.provider: Biodiversity Heritage Library (Smithsonian Libraries and Archives host)
resources.free_notes: Home page states its aim as free access to biodiversity knowledge. I could not open a licence page, so check each item's rights field; most older volumes are public domain (my background knowledge, not verified). A Flickr stream of about 320,000 plate images exists at flickr.com/photos/biodivlibrary (count shown on the page; per-image rights label not visible to me).
resources.notes: Browse botanical plates to see how historical illustrators show leaf undersides, cut stems and flower dissections on one sheet. Search for a plant you can also find in a local park.

practice.title: Paper-model leaf bends
practice.description: Fold sheets of paper into leaves and petals, then draw each from several angles, as in the Laws series.

practice.title: Leaf arrangement sheet
practice.description: Draw five stems, each using a different leaf arrangement (alternate, opposite, whorled, spiral, rosette).

practice.title: Flower from three views
practice.description: Pick one flower and draw it from the side, at three-quarter and from above, showing how petals attach to the centre.

practice.title: Fork study
practice.description: Draw ten branch forks from a real twig, showing how thickness drops after each split.

practice.title: Plate copy
practice.description: Copy part of a botanical plate from BHL to see how overlaps and cut sections are shown. For study only; do not publish the copy as your own.

practice.title: Invent a plant
practice.description: Combine growth rules you have drawn (spiral leaves, forking stems, rosettes) into three made-up plants.

done_when: You can draw a leaf from three angles so it reads as a bent plane, not an outline
Your branches thin sensibly after each fork
You can name and sketch at least four leaf arrangements from memory
You can draw a flower you have not studied before, using a simple form to place the petals
One invented plant gets a believable answer when someone asks how it would grow
common_mistakes: Drawing every leaf flat and facing the viewer, same size and angle
Ignoring where the stem joins the leaf or the branch, so parts look glued on
Adding vein and edge detail before the leaf's overall bend is right
Giving every branch the same thickness

school_reference.note: Paid in-person course: Fundamentals of botanical illustration is 5 days, 470 GBP for adults (460 GBP Kew Members) in Oct 2026; it teaches accurate flower and leaf drawing by measurement and perspective, then watercolour. Kew also lists pen-and-ink courses for beginners and intermediate students. Useful as an ordering model: structure and measurement first, then ink or colour.

title: Insects, arachnids and small creatures
summary: Small animals have a clear body plan, so they are good practice for building forms from sections. You draw insects with a head, thorax and abdomen, jointed legs and wings, and spiders with two body sections and eight legs, then add shiny, matte and iridescent surfaces.
learning_outcomes: Divide an insect or spider into its body sections and place them in perspective
Draw jointed legs as segmented tubes attached at the correct body part
Foreshorten a beetle or bug from above, front and three-quarter views
Show wing structure for butterflies and dragonflies
Render shiny, dull and iridescent shells with a few value shapes

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Insects (legs, foreshortening, shiny and iridescent surfaces)
resources.free_notes: No paywall on the page and the site metadata calls the tutorials free. A worksheet is described as free but links to a /product/ URL; I could not see a price.
resources.notes: Order: 'How to Draw Insects' (video workshop), then the two-part leg lessons (understanding and drawing the legs), 'Drawing foreshortened insects: Seven-spotted Ladybug', 'shiny vs. dull textures', 'Iridescence', then 'Spider anatomy for artists'. Finish with a butterfly or dragonfly lesson.

resources.title: Drawabox Lesson 4: Applying Construction to Insects and Arachnids
resources.free_notes: Drawabox's server returned a bot-check page to my fetch, so I could not read the lesson or any price. The lesson title is confirmed from public community submission titles, and the /lesson/N URL pattern is confirmed by lesson 7 appearing in search results. Whether instructor critique sits behind a paid or supporter tier is not verified.
resources.notes: Use after Laws's leg lessons if you want a strict construction routine. The lesson is about building insect and arachnid forms from basic shapes in 3D.

resources.title: Museums Victoria Collections (Melbourne zoology, geology and palaeontology records)
resources.free_notes: About page: record data is CC0, curator text is CC BY 4.0, and images are licensed separately with over 100,000 openly licensed or public domain. Check the licence on each image.
resources.notes: Search the Melbourne museum's zoology records for beetles, spiders and butterflies. Many have photographed specimens you can rotate through in different views; check each image licence.

resources.title: Smithsonian Open Access (5.2 million+ images including National Zoo and natural history)
resources.free_notes: Page says millions of images can be downloaded, shared and reused without asking and links to a CC0 filter. Page also says the collection holds more than 5.2 million 2D and 3D items.
resources.notes: Filter to CC0 and search for entomology specimen photos when you want side-by-side views of the same species.

practice.title: Legs as segmented tubes
practice.description: Draw six insects with every leg built as joined tube segments that start at the thorax, not the abdomen.

practice.title: Beetle from three angles
practice.description: Draw one beetle from above, front and three-quarter, keeping body proportions consistent.

practice.title: Spider body plan
practice.description: Draw three spiders with two body sections, eight jointed legs and paired mouthparts, from live subjects or specimen photos.

practice.title: Wing study
practice.description: Draw one butterfly and one dragonfly wing pair, tracing the vein pattern as a network of large shapes before small ones.

practice.title: Texture ladder
practice.description: Render one shiny beetle, one matte bug and one iridescent insect, using as few value shapes as you can.

practice.title: Specimen page
practice.description: Fill one page with eight insects at relative scale, labelled with where you saw them or found the reference.

done_when: Every insect you draw has three body sections and legs attached to the middle one
Spiders you draw have two body sections and eight legs
A foreshortened beetle still reads as one solid object
You can render a shiny shell using a small number of value shapes
common_mistakes: Attaching legs to the abdomen or to random places along the body
Drawing legs as single thin lines with no joints
Giving spiders six or ten legs, or a single blob body
Drawing only flat top views so the insect never turns in space

school_reference.note: Not a school: an open zoology collection with specimen photos and licences. Useful as a local reference source.

title: Mammal anatomy and construction (quadrupeds, comparison with human anatomy)
summary: Build four-legged animals from a ribcage, a pelvis and a head mass, then attach limbs made of the same kinds of bones we have, in different proportions. Comparing a dog or horse limb with a human arm or leg explains why animal joints bend the way they do.
learning_outcomes: Block in a quadruped from ribcage, pelvis, neck and head masses
Place the shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle equivalents in a dog or cat leg
Compare a hoofed, a paw-footed and a human limb on one page
Draw a mammal head including nose and ears from several angles
Add fur direction after the structure is correct

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Mammals (bear, deer, mountain lion, fox, wolves, bats, comparative leg anatomy)
resources.free_notes: Page opened: no paywall, price or login shown, but it does not itself say the tutorials are free. Sister pages (plants, insects, birds) state in their metadata that the tutorials are free. A downloadable muscle worksheet, the store and an educator certification link exist; prices not shown.
resources.notes: Follow one animal at a time in his pattern: 'How to Block in the Basic Shape' of a deer or bear, then the muscular anatomy lesson (bear, deer, mountain lion), then the fur texture lesson. Then do 'How to Draw Mammals: Comparative Anatomy of the Legs', 'Mammal Noses' and 'Mammal Ears'. Sidebar extras: Wolves, Bats, 'Drawing Mammal Heads: Predator vs. Prey'.

resources.title: Aaron Blaise: How to Draw Animals (dog, wolf, cat, horse, polar bear videos)
resources.credit: Aaron Blaise (former Disney animator), channel 'The Art of Aaron Blaise'
resources.free_notes: Wacom's article embeds five public YouTube videos. Blaise's own site says his YouTube channel carries hundreds of hours of free content and labels a cat lesson as free. His full courses at creatureartteacher.com are paid (pay-what-you-want bundles from 5 USD were shown during a sale).
resources.notes: Watch the dog and wolf videos first, then cat and horse, then polar bear. While watching, note what he draws first and where he places the leg joints; then redraw from reference without the video. Direct links: dogs youtube.com/watch?v=zT46ZaoO_pE, wolf youtube.com/watch?v=vYcSRs_ppdo, horse youtube.com/watch?v=F1qycYD40Dc.

resources.title: Drawabox Lesson 5: Applying Construction to Animals
resources.free_notes: Drawabox's server returned a bot-check page to my fetch, so I could not read the lesson or any price. The lesson title is confirmed from public community submission titles, and the /lesson/N URL pattern is confirmed by lesson 7 appearing in search results. Whether instructor critique sits behind a paid or supporter tier is not verified.
resources.notes: Use for the construction-first method on animals. Follow it after the Laws lessons, since Drawabox is far stricter and more demanding.

resources.title: Smithsonian 3D (rotatable models of skulls, fossils, bones)
resources.free_notes: Free to explore in the browser. The page does not state a licence; terms are on si.edu/Termsofuse. Use for study only unless you check terms.
resources.notes: Rotate skulls and bones to see the shapes your constructions stand in for. Pick a mammal skull and draw it from front, side and three-quarter.

practice.title: Block-in then anatomy
practice.description: Draw one mammal in three passes: simple volumes, then bones and muscle masses, then surface. Repeat for a second animal.

practice.title: Limb comparison page
practice.description: On one page draw a human arm, a dog foreleg and a horse foreleg with the same joints marked, so you can see how the shapes change.

practice.title: Skull studies
practice.description: Draw two mammal skulls from front, side and three-quarter from a 3D model.

practice.title: Torso-and-limbs speed constructions
practice.description: Make quick constructions of different quadrupeds starting from ribcage and pelvis boxes, then add limbs.

practice.title: Head parts
practice.description: Draw six mammal noses and ears from different species and angles.

practice.title: Zoo or photo session
practice.description: Draw four animals from a photo set of a zoo animal, reducing each to masses before detail.

done_when: You can block in a standing dog, cat or horse from memory with believable proportions
You can mark the equivalents of shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee and ankle on a quadruped leg
Your animal heads are built from simple forms, not outlined as flat shapes
You can draw a limb comparison page without copying
common_mistakes: Sticking legs onto the body outline instead of connecting them to the shoulder and hip masses
Misreading the 'backward knee' on a hind leg, which is actually the ankle
Making the ribcage as small as the pelvis, so the torso looks stuffed
Adding fur texture to a shape that is still wrong

title: Birds
summary: Birds are an egg-like body, a small head, a wing that folds into layers and a leg that hides its upper bones. You build birds from the basic shape first, then learn feather groups, wing folds, flight poses, and how different species change the proportions.
learning_outcomes: Draw a perched bird from an egg-like body, head circle and tail line
Show folded wings as layered feather groups rather than single feathers
Place the leg correctly and recognise the ankle as the apparent backward knee
Sketch a bird in under 90 seconds from live observation
Adapt proportions for ducks, hawks, owls and small songbirds

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Birds (intro, hawks, owls, feather groups, flight)
resources.free_notes: Site metadata calls the tutorials free; no paywall seen. The sparrow worksheet and the book 'The Laws Guide to Drawing Birds' are separate store products with no price visible to me.
resources.notes: Order on the page: 'Introduction to Drawing Birds' (White-throated Sparrow), 'Start with the Basic Shape', 'Look Below the Surface', 'Learn to See Feather Groups', 'Birds Are Shape Shifters', then hawks and owls. Add '60-Second Bird Sketching', 'Gesture Sketching Birds' and 'Simplifying Bird Wings' from the sidebar.

resources.title: Atlas of Living Australia (species pages with community photos)
resources.credit: Atlas of Living Australia and individual photographers
resources.free_notes: Open-access biodiversity data platform. Photos carry individual Creative Commons licences, some CC BY and some CC BY-NC, so check each photo before reusing anything beyond private study.
resources.notes: Search a common local bird and choose a species page with several photos from different angles. Check each photo's licence; some are CC BY-NC.

resources.title: Cornell Lab Bird Academy: Nature Journaling and Field Sketching (plus free webinars)
resources.provider: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Bird Academy
resources.free_notes: Nature Journaling and Field Sketching and How to Paint Birds with Jane Kim were each listed at 99.99 USD in Oct 2026. Some webinars on the same site are free (for example a live sketching session with Liz Clayton Fuller). Use as supplementary only.
resources.notes: Paid courses on bird painting and field sketching. Free webinars on the same site occasionally cover drawing. Optional.

practice.title: Sixty-second birds
practice.description: Sketch perched birds in one-minute bursts, focusing on body shape and head angle, from live birds or video.

practice.title: Egg-and-head builds
practice.description: Build six different birds from an egg-like body, head circle and tail line, then add the beak and leg.

practice.title: Wing layer map
practice.description: Draw three closed wings and mark the feather groups (small coverts, large coverts, flight feathers) as stacked shapes.

practice.title: Silhouette comparison
practice.description: Draw duck, hawk, owl and warbler silhouettes at similar scale to see which proportions change.

practice.title: Birds in odd views
practice.description: Draw birds from below, from behind and in flight, using photos or video frames of the same species.

practice.title: Local bird page
practice.description: Spend one outing sketching the most common bird near you and add three notes about posture and behaviour.

done_when: You can draw a recognisable perched bird in under 90 seconds
Folded wings are shown as stacked groups, not a pile of single feathers
Legs and ankles come out of the body at the right place and bend the right way
Different species show different proportions in your sketches
common_mistakes: Drawing feathers one by one before the body shape is right
Making the head too big or the neck too stiff
Putting legs in the middle of the belly instead of low and slightly back
Making the wing a flat paddle with no layering

school_reference.institution: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Bird Academy
school_reference.note: Course catalogue includes field sketching and bird painting (paid, 99.99 USD each listed Oct 2026). Syllabi not read.

title: Reptiles, amphibians and fish
summary: These animals use different body plans from mammals: sprawling limbs, a spine-led S curve, streamlined cross-sections and patterned skin. You learn to build them from volumes, then place scales, fins and eyes. This is the thinnest area for free structured teaching, so it relies on method transfer and reference.
learning_outcomes: Build a lizard, snake, frog or fish from a spine line and body volumes
Show lizard limbs attached to the side of the body with a sprawl
Draw fish as streamlined cross-sections with fins placed correctly
Render scale patterns that follow the form
Observe from specimen photos and plates

resources.title: Drawabox Lesson 5: Applying Construction to Animals
resources.free_notes: Drawabox's server returned a bot-check page to my fetch, so I could not read the lesson or any price. The lesson title is confirmed from public community submission titles, and the /lesson/N URL pattern is confirmed by lesson 7 appearing in search results. Whether instructor critique sits behind a paid or supporter tier is not verified.
resources.notes: Treat the animal lesson as a method for any creature: build large forms, add joints and masses, then details. Apply it to a lizard, frog and fish yourself. No dedicated free reptile or fish course was found, which is why this module is thin.

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Mammals (bear, deer, mountain lion, fox, wolves, bats, comparative leg anatomy)
resources.free_notes: Page opened: no paywall, price or login shown, but it does not itself say the tutorials are free. Sister pages (plants, insects, birds) state in their metadata that the tutorials are free. A downloadable muscle worksheet, the store and an educator certification link exist; prices not shown.
resources.notes: Use the three-pass routine (block in, anatomy, texture) from the bear and deer lessons on a reptile or fish instead of a mammal.

resources.title: Ernst Haeckel, Kunstformen der Natur (Art Forms in Nature, 1899-1904, 100 plates)
resources.free_notes: Scan links come from the Wikipedia article for the work (BHL item 182319, Internet Archive KunstformenderN00Haec, a BHL Flickr album). I did not open each. Haeckel died in 1919, so the plates are old enough to be public domain in most countries.
resources.notes: Browse Haeckel's plates for fish, sea creatures and radiolarian forms and copy one as a pattern study; also a strong source for invented marine creatures.

resources.title: Museums Victoria Collections (Melbourne zoology, geology and palaeontology records)
resources.free_notes: About page: record data is CC0, curator text is CC BY 4.0, and images are licensed separately with over 100,000 openly licensed or public domain. Check the licence on each image.
resources.notes: Search the Melbourne zoology records for reptiles, frogs and fish and check image licences. Several species pages should include whole-animal views.

practice.title: Spine-first reptiles
practice.description: Draw a lizard, a snake and a crocodile from one S-curved spine with the limbs sprawling to the sides.

practice.title: Fish volumes
practice.description: Draw six fish side views and two head-on views, placing the fins as thin planes attached to the body.

practice.title: Scale rows
practice.description: Fill two patches with scales as curved overlapping rows that turn with the surface, not random dots.

practice.title: Frog legs folded
practice.description: Draw a frog's folded hind legs from three angles, tracking each joint.

practice.title: Plate study
practice.description: Choose one fish or reptile plate from BHL and redraw it at half size, matching the overlaps.

practice.title: Eyes and mouths
practice.description: Draw six eyes and mouths of different species (slit pupil, bulging frog eye, fish eye) in close-up.

done_when: Your lizards sprawl and your snakes bend through an S line rather than staying straight
A fish you draw has a believable cross-section, not just a flat outline
Scale patterns wrap the form
You have one reference-based study of each group (reptile, amphibian, fish)
common_mistakes: Giving a lizard mammal-style legs directly under the body
Making snakes uniform tubes with no taper or head structure
Drawing fish as flat outlines with no volume
Painting scales as identical dots that ignore the form turning

school_reference.note: Lists US and non-US science illustration programmes (the list did not render for me). Handbook and Recordings pages exist; access terms not stated.

title: Animal gesture, locomotion and expression
summary: Move from still structure to movement: how an animal's spine, weight and limbs flow through a walk, run or leap, and how ears, eyes, tail and posture signal mood. You use fast gesture drawing, photo sequences of animals in motion, and live cams.
learning_outcomes: Capture the action line and weight of an animal in 30 to 60 seconds
Break a walk, trot and gallop into key phases using sequence photos
Show weight shift and balance, not just limb positions
Read and draw expression through ears, eyes, tail and posture
Combine a few quick sketches into a short movement study

resources.title: Aaron Blaise: How to Draw Animals (dog, wolf, cat, horse, polar bear videos)
resources.credit: Aaron Blaise (former Disney animator), channel 'The Art of Aaron Blaise'
resources.free_notes: Wacom's article embeds five public YouTube videos. Blaise's own site says his YouTube channel carries hundreds of hours of free content and labels a cat lesson as free. His full courses at creatureartteacher.com are paid (pay-what-you-want bundles from 5 USD were shown during a sale).
resources.notes: Use the dog, wolf and horse videos to watch how a pose is built from large shapes. Then draw the same animals moving, from video, using gesture, not outline. Direct links: wolf youtube.com/watch?v=vYcSRs_ppdo, horse youtube.com/watch?v=F1qycYD40Dc.

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Birds (intro, hawks, owls, feather groups, flight)
resources.free_notes: Site metadata calls the tutorials free; no paywall seen. The sparrow worksheet and the book 'The Laws Guide to Drawing Birds' are separate store products with no price visible to me.
resources.notes: Study 'Gesture Sketching Birds', '60-Second Bird Sketching' and 'Birds in Flight with Peter Cavanagh' from the sidebar. The same speed-first approach applies to mammals.

resources.title: Muybridge, Animal Locomotion (1887) on Wikimedia Commons
resources.free_notes: Commons category groups the 11 volumes of plates (horses, domestic and wild animals, birds, and humans). Licence is shown per file; plates from 1887 by an author who died in 1904 are expected to be public domain but confirm on each file page.
resources.notes: Use the horse and animal plates as time-slice reference: thumbnail the leg positions across a walk, trot and gallop, then draw a pose from your thumbnails.

resources.title: explore.org live nature cams (bears, birds, oceans, Africa)
resources.free_notes: Network of live animal cams. The page lists YouTube channels for bears, oceans, eagles and birds, and Africa; it does not state fees, so confirm access per cam. Use for gesture practice only; do not copy frames for publication.
resources.notes: Pick a live bear, bird or ocean cam and do timed gesture drawings of whatever moves into frame. Cost per cam not stated; use as practice only.

practice.title: Live-cam gestures
practice.description: Draw moving animals from a live cam in 30-second bursts, line of action first, then body masses.

practice.title: Gait breakdown
practice.description: Draw eight thumbnails of a horse walk and gallop from sequence plates, marking which feet are down.

practice.title: Weight and balance pair
practice.description: Draw the same animal standing relaxed and about to move, changing only weight distribution.

practice.title: Expression sheet
practice.description: Draw one dog or cat in six moods (alert, relaxed, fearful, playful, annoyed, sleepy) by watching real animals or video.

practice.title: Action line-ups
practice.description: Do twelve two-minute poses of different animals, using one flowing line for the spine before anything else.

practice.title: Bird flight sequence
practice.description: From a video, draw six frames of a bird's wing beat as simple shapes.

done_when: You can draw a believable animal pose in 60 seconds with a clear action line
Your gallop drawings show the correct phases of the stride, not all four feet planted
Two drawings of the same animal can show different moods through ears, eyes and tail alone
You can sketch from live observation without needing a photo
common_mistakes: Drawing the outline of each limb and skipping the spine's flow
Putting all four feet on the ground in a gallop or leap
Using human facial logic (brows, mouth) for animals instead of ears, eyes and tail
Spending five minutes on a pose meant to take thirty seconds

title: Fur, feather, scale and shell textures
summary: An extra module for rendering surfaces on animals once the structure is right. You learn to show direction and clumping in fur, layering in feathers, overlap in scales and the difference between shiny and matte shells, using as few marks as you can.
learning_outcomes: Draw fur in clumps that follow the form and direction of growth
Layer feathers from small to large in groups
Render scales, shells and iridescence using a handful of value shapes
Change mark type to match the material (fur, feather, scale, chitin)

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Mammals (bear, deer, mountain lion, fox, wolves, bats, comparative leg anatomy)
resources.free_notes: Page opened: no paywall, price or login shown, but it does not itself say the tutorials are free. Sister pages (plants, insects, birds) state in their metadata that the tutorials are free. A downloadable muscle worksheet, the store and an educator certification link exist; prices not shown.
resources.notes: Do the three fur texture lessons (Bear, Deer, Mountain Lion) after finishing the muscular anatomy lessons for the same animal.

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Birds (intro, hawks, owls, feather groups, flight)
resources.free_notes: Site metadata calls the tutorials free; no paywall seen. The sparrow worksheet and the book 'The Laws Guide to Drawing Birds' are separate store products with no price visible to me.
resources.notes: Use 'Learn to See Feather Groups' and 'Drawing Iridescent Birds' (sidebar) for feather layering and sheen.

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Insects (legs, foreshortening, shiny and iridescent surfaces)
resources.free_notes: No paywall on the page and the site metadata calls the tutorials free. A worksheet is described as free but links to a /product/ URL; I could not see a price.
resources.notes: 'How to draw insects: shiny vs. dull textures' and 'Iridescence' apply the same logic to shells.

resources.title: Alphonso Dunn: pen and ink, urban sketching and landscape tutorials (YouTube)
resources.free_notes: Channel describes free drawing tutorials. His books and any courses are paid. The page summary mentioned playlists on trees, landscapes, perspective and architecture, but I could not confirm exact playlist names, so search the channel.
resources.notes: Search his pen-and-ink texture videos for hatching and stippling approaches to fur and scale. Exact video titles not confirmed by me.

practice.title: Fur direction map
practice.description: On a quick animal drawing, mark fur direction with a few long strokes before adding any texture.

practice.title: Feather layering
practice.description: Draw a fanned wing as three stacked rows of feathers, one row at a time.

practice.title: Scale patch
practice.description: Draw a patch of scales that curves with a cylinder or sphere.

practice.title: Shell sheen
practice.description: Render a beetle shell as matte, shiny and iridescent versions using a limited set of tones.

practice.title: Material swap
practice.description: Draw the same simple form (a sphere) covered in fur, feathers and scales.

done_when: Fur reads as clumps with direction, not as scribbles
Feather drawings show layers and groups
A scale patch turns with the surface
You can change your marks for a different material without redoing the structure
common_mistakes: Drawing every hair or feather at full detail across the whole animal
Using the same mark for fur, feathers and scales
Adding texture on top of wrong anatomy and hoping it hides the problem
Making the whole surface equally sharp

title: Creature design: inventing believable animals and hybrids
summary: An extra module aimed at surreal and invented work. You borrow real anatomy, growth logic and locomotion to design creatures that seem able to live, and study imaginative illustrators such as Heinrich Kley and Ernst Haeckel for ideas on the strange and the ornamental.
learning_outcomes: Design a creature by mixing parts of real animals at the joint and muscle level
Give a made-up animal a plausible gait, diet and body plan
Use scale, pattern and silhouette to make a creature distinctive
Borrow ideas from natural-history plates and early imaginative illustration without copying them

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Mammals (bear, deer, mountain lion, fox, wolves, bats, comparative leg anatomy)
resources.free_notes: Page opened: no paywall, price or login shown, but it does not itself say the tutorials are free. Sister pages (plants, insects, birds) state in their metadata that the tutorials are free. A downloadable muscle worksheet, the store and an educator certification link exist; prices not shown.
resources.notes: Use the comparative anatomy of legs, noses and ears lessons as a toolkit of real forms to mix. No free structured creature-design course was verified, so this is a method transfer.

resources.title: Ernst Haeckel, Kunstformen der Natur (Art Forms in Nature, 1899-1904, 100 plates)
resources.free_notes: Scan links come from the Wikipedia article for the work (BHL item 182319, Internet Archive KunstformenderN00Haec, a BHL Flickr album). I did not open each. Haeckel died in 1919, so the plates are old enough to be public domain in most countries.
resources.notes: Study the plates for symmetry, spirals and ornament that inspire alien or deep-sea creatures. Pick three plates and note what makes each silhouette distinct.

resources.title: Heinrich Kley (Wikipedia): biography and bibliography
resources.free_notes: Free to read. The article lists his sketchbooks (Skizzenbuch I and II, Leut' und Viecher) and the Dover reprints, which are in print and paid. Death date is disputed (1945 most likely, one source says 1952). I found no verified free scan collection of his drawings.
resources.notes: Read the biography for context on his work, then search Wikimedia Commons or the Internet Archive yourself for his sketchbooks; I did not verify a free scan collection, so check the licence shown on any copy.

resources.title: The Gnomon Workshop: Creature Design with Terryl Whitlatch, Vol. 3
resources.free_notes: Paid workshop; price not checked. Her book 'Science of Creature Design: Understanding Animal Anatomy' is also paid. Supplementary only.
resources.notes: Paid workshop from a working creature designer. Use only if you want a structured alternative; the free path above should come first.

practice.title: Anatomy mix-and-match
practice.description: Pick two real animals, list three body features of each, and draw a hybrid that keeps the joints and muscles working.

practice.title: Gait for a made-up body
practice.description: Draw a four-panel walk cycle for one invented creature, explaining which limbs lead.

practice.title: Silhouette thumbnails
practice.description: Thumbnail twenty silhouettes of invented creatures and pick the three most distinct.

practice.title: Plate-inspired creature
practice.description: Choose a Haeckel plate and design a creature whose body repeats its pattern.

practice.title: Habitat note
practice.description: Write three sentences about where one of your creatures lives and what it eats, then adjust the drawing to match.

practice.title: Turnaround
practice.description: Draw one creature in front, side and back views with consistent proportions.

done_when: A hybrid creature has joints and limbs that could physically work
Your silhouettes are different enough to tell apart at thumbnail size
You can draw one invented creature from three consistent views
You can explain what it eats and how it moves
common_mistakes: Gluing parts together without adjusting the skeleton or proportions
Adding spikes and horns everywhere instead of designing one strong feature
Copying a historic plate or Kley drawing instead of borrowing a principle
Skipping thumbnails and falling for the first idea

title: Landscape elements: rocks, mountains, terrain, clouds, water, fire and smoke
summary: Natural elements without a fixed shape need rules instead of outlines: rocks as a few planes, mountains as layered masses, clouds as lit volumes, water as reflection and movement, fire and smoke as flowing shapes. You practise each element in isolation before putting them in a scene.
learning_outcomes: Reduce a rock or cliff to three to five planes with a light direction
Layer mountains and hills to suggest distance
Draw clouds as lit three-dimensional masses and name the main types
Show calm water, ripples and reflections correctly
Draw fire and smoke as moving shapes with a clear flow

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Landscapes (clouds, trees, water, forests)
resources.free_notes: No prices shown on the page. One entry, 'Class: Learn to Draw Water with John Muir Laws', reads like a paid class; the individual workshop posts appear open. No lesson here is specifically about mountains.
resources.notes: Clouds: 'How to Draw Cloud Shapes', then 'How to Draw Clouds in Perspective'. Water: 'How to Draw Creeks and Moving Water', 'How to Draw Water: Open Ocean', 'How to Draw Sea Foam', 'The Mountain Stream', 'Coastal Cliffs and Waves'. Rocks and mountains have no dedicated lesson there; use photo studies.

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint free video library (hundreds of short lessons)
resources.free_notes: Site says the free library has hundreds of streaming videos, about 5 minutes each, ordered from basic to advanced. Individual extra videos are sold at 10 USD each in the store. I could not confirm category names, so use it for painting and values rather than as a drawing curriculum.
resources.notes: Use the free library for short lessons on values, edges and colour that apply to skies and terrain. I could not confirm category names, so browse for landscape or environment videos and treat it as supplementary.

resources.title: WMO International Cloud Atlas (official cloud types, photos and definitions)
resources.free_notes: Public website; the page footer reads 2017 WMO copyright and I saw no open licence, so use for looking and naming clouds, not for reuse. The page does not state fees.
resources.notes: Look up the standard cloud genera and species and pick six to draw from photos. Use for naming and reference only.

resources.title: Unsplash licence (free photos)
resources.free_notes: Licence page: free for commercial and noncommercial use, no permission or attribution required. Not allowed: compiling images into a competing service.
resources.notes: Free photo source (licence page checked). Search for mountains, rocks, waterfalls, campfires and smoke to build your own reference set; check the photo credit and keep the link.

practice.title: Cloud type sheet
practice.description: Draw six clouds from photos, naming each type and marking the light side and shadow side.

practice.title: Rock planes
practice.description: Reduce ten rocks or cliffs to three to five flat planes each, with one light direction.

practice.title: Mountain layers
practice.description: Draw three mountain scenes with three overlapping ridges in separate values.

practice.title: Water pair
practice.description: Draw one calm reflection and one moving stream; note how reflection shapes change with ripples.

practice.title: Fire and smoke flow
practice.description: Draw ten flame and smoke studies from photos, using one flowing line per mass.

practice.title: Terrain thumbnails
practice.description: Thumbnail six landscape compositions combining rock, water and sky.

done_when: Your rocks and cliffs read as solid with a single consistent light direction
Mountains in your drawings recede through value and overlap
Clouds look like volumes with a lit side
Reflections sit under their objects and respond to ripples
Smoke and flame drawings show flow, not outlines
common_mistakes: Outlining clouds like cotton wool
Drawing mountains as symmetrical triangles with equal detail everywhere
Making reflections the wrong size or ignoring the horizon
Keeping the same sharpness at all distances

title: Foliage and trees in landscape scenes
summary: Trees in a scene are masses, silhouettes and rhythms, not collections of leaves. You study species shapes and how to build a canopy as groups, then place trees in layered scenes with depth, light and seasons.
learning_outcomes: Draw several tree types (oak, conifer, aspen, bare winter tree) as distinct silhouettes
Build foliage in clumps with one light side and a shadow side
Show a forest in layers of foreground, middle and background
Place trees in a scene without making them look pasted on

resources.title: John Muir Laws: How to Draw Landscapes (clouds, trees, water, forests)
resources.free_notes: No prices shown on the page. One entry, 'Class: Learn to Draw Water with John Muir Laws', reads like a paid class; the individual workshop posts appear open. No lesson here is specifically about mountains.
resources.notes: Trees section: 'Drawing Deciduous Trees' (video), 'Let's draw Oak Trees!', 'How to Draw Aspen and Steal Inspiration', 'How to Draw Coniferous Forests', 'How to draw an Oak Woodland', 'How to Draw Trees in Winter', 'How to draw a Forest' (video).

resources.title: Botanical Art and Artists: tips on drawing trees and leaves, plus sketchbook and pencil video tips
resources.free_notes: Page opened: a hub on leaf shape, veination and arrangement (phyllotaxis), leaf colour and watercolour technique, plus bark, twigs and buds and how to observe and plan tree drawings. Site describes itself as free to the reader and earns Amazon affiliate commission on book links. The same site also sells online courses and diplomas.
resources.notes: Use the trees-and-leaves hub for bark, twigs and buds, and its tips on observing, measuring and planning a tree drawing; it is botanical rather than landscape, so use it to understand structure before you simplify.

resources.title: Alphonso Dunn: pen and ink, urban sketching and landscape tutorials (YouTube)
resources.free_notes: Channel describes free drawing tutorials. His books and any courses are paid. The page summary mentioned playlists on trees, landscapes, perspective and architecture, but I could not confirm exact playlist names, so search the channel.
resources.notes: Search the channel for tree and landscape pen-and-ink videos and follow one tree and one forest scene start to finish. Exact titles unconfirmed.

resources.title: Citizen Sketcher: step-by-step demos
resources.free_notes: Downloads page opened: seven free PDFs, including 'Making Expressive Pen and Ink Drawings on Location' (11 pages, made with the Virginia Center for Architecture for an architect audience), 'The Broken Silhouette', 'Drawing People in Motion' and 'Actors on Stage'. None covers perspective. A Free Videos category also exists. His online classes page (citizensketcher.com/videos/) is not marked free; his books and downloadable video classes elsewhere are paid.
resources.notes: Browse for scenes that include trees and see how a field sketcher places them with a few large marks. Page contents not opened.

practice.title: Tree silhouette set
practice.description: Draw eight tree silhouettes (oak, pine, aspen, eucalypt, bare winter tree, palm, willow, cypress) in solid black.

practice.title: Clump foliage
practice.description: Draw one tree canopy as three to five clumps, each with a light side and a shadow side.

practice.title: Bare tree structure
practice.description: Draw a leafless tree focusing on how trunk, main limbs and twigs thin out.

practice.title: Forest layers
practice.description: Draw a forest in three value layers: foreground trunks, middle trees, pale background.

practice.title: Tree in a field
practice.description: Draw a lone tree with a cast shadow on the ground and a horizon behind it.

done_when: Different tree species are recognisable from their silhouette alone
Your canopies are built from masses with a light direction
A forest scene has at least three clear depth layers
Trees in your scenes cast shadows and sit on the ground
common_mistakes: Drawing individual leaves everywhere
Making every tree the same shape and size
Using the same value for distant and near trees
Planting trees with no shadow or ground contact

title: Everyday objects and product forms: containers, tools, furniture, bottles, fabric objects
summary: Ordinary objects are built from cylinders, boxes and spheres with handles, hinges and openings added. You practise ellipses for bottles and cups, boxes for furniture, simple mechanisms for tools, and soft shapes for bags and cushions. Fabric folds overlap with drapery in the figure group.
learning_outcomes: Build bottles, cups and jugs from cylinders with consistent ellipses
Attach handles, spouts and lids so they feel solid
Draw a chair and table from boxes in two-point perspective
Draw simple tools and hinges with believable thickness
Show a bag or cushion with a few sensible folds

resources.title: Drawabox Lesson 6: Drawing Everyday Objects
resources.free_notes: Drawabox's server returned a bot-check page to my fetch, so I could not read the lesson or any price. The lesson title is confirmed from public community submission titles, and the /lesson/N URL pattern is confirmed by lesson 7 appearing in search results. Whether instructor critique sits behind a paid or supporter tier is not verified.
resources.notes: Do this lesson after you are comfortable with boxes and ellipses. It asks for objects from your own home built with construction methods, which is better practice than copying from a photo.

resources.title: Eric Strebel: industrial design and product development (YouTube)
resources.free_notes: Public YouTube channel about industrial design, prototyping and product techniques. Sketching appeared only as a channel keyword, so I could not confirm which videos teach drawing. He teaches industrial design at Wayne State University and CCS.
resources.notes: Browse the channel for videos on sketching objects and for how designers think about product form. Content for sketching unconfirmed; skim titles before committing.

resources.title: The Met Open Access (492,000+ works, CC0)
resources.free_notes: Met states public-domain images and data are CC0, over 492,000 works, flagged with an OA icon in the online collection.
resources.notes: Search the Open Access collection for vessels, furniture, tools and decorative objects in CC0 images. Good for seeing the same object type in different designs.

resources.title: Rijksmuseum online collection (high-resolution downloads, Dutch still life and design)
resources.free_notes: Page says all freely available works can be downloaded in high resolution for personal and commercial use. It does not name CC0 on that page.
resources.notes: Use for historic objects and still-life paintings with many everyday items. Free to download in high resolution.

practice.title: Cylinder family
practice.description: Draw eight containers (bottle, mug, jug, jar, tin, vase, glass, bucket) from cylinders with consistent ellipse openness.

practice.title: Handle and spout attach
practice.description: Draw five objects with handles or spouts, constructing them in 3D before outlining.

practice.title: Furniture from boxes
practice.description: Draw a chair and a table from simple boxes in two-point perspective, then add legs and thickness.

practice.title: Tools and hinges
practice.description: Draw a pair of scissors, pliers and a hammer showing thickness and pivot points.

practice.title: Soft goods
practice.description: Draw a bag, a cushion and a scarf draped over a chair, finding the tension lines.

practice.title: Three-view product
practice.description: Pick one object and draw front, side and top views at the same scale.

done_when: Ellipses on a stack of cylinders get progressively rounder as they sit lower, if viewed from above
Handles and spouts meet the body convincingly in every angle
Furniture sits flat with legs landing in the right places
A bag or cushion shows believable folds and weight
common_mistakes: Making ellipse axes tilt randomly, so a cup looks wobbly
Letting handles float without a join
Drawing furniture without thickness
Adding detail before the silhouette and volume are right

title: Hard-surface and mechanical forms: vehicles, machines, robots
summary: Cars, aircraft, ships, machines and robots combine boxes, cylinders and curved surfaces with panel lines, wheels and joints. You learn to use ellipses for wheels, to build a car's body as a few large volumes, and to design from silhouette, drawing on automotive design practice.
learning_outcomes: Draw wheels as correct ellipses in perspective, front and rear
Block in a car with a few large volumes before panel lines
Sketch aircraft or boats from a side-view silhouette and a cross-section
Design a simple robot or machine from primitive forms and joints
Add panel lines that follow the form

resources.title: Petersen Automotive Museum x Yellowbrick: Auto Design course (3 modules, incl. Let's Draw!)
resources.credit: Petersen Automotive Museum; sketching module taught by Prof. Roman Yneges (ArtCenter College of Design)
resources.free_notes: Sign-up page says to enter an email address to start for free. Press coverage at the time (The Drive) also called it free. Self-paced lessons of roughly 6 to 15 minutes. Only sketching materials needed for module 3.
resources.notes: Take module 3, 'Let's Draw!' with Prof. Roman Yneges (ArtCenter): perspective, circles and ellipses, then classic and modern cars. Watch modules 1 and 2 first if you want the history and case studies (DeLorean, Lamborghini Gallardo, Ford Shelby Mustang, Tesla Model S).

resources.title: Drawabox Lesson 7: Applying Construction to Vehicles
resources.free_notes: Drawabox's server returned a bot-check page to my fetch, so I could not read the lesson or any price. The lesson title is confirmed from public community submission titles, and the /lesson/N URL pattern is confirmed by lesson 7 appearing in search results. Whether instructor critique sits behind a paid or supporter tier is not verified.
resources.notes: Use for construction-first drawing of vehicles of many kinds. Follow after the Petersen lessons, as it asks for a lot of homework.

resources.title: FZD School of Design YouTube channel (concept design tutorials for games and film)
resources.provider: Feng Zhu Design School (FZD School of Design)
resources.free_notes: YouTube channel is public and self-described as concept design tutorials for games and film. Paid courses and the school itself are at fzdschool.com (prices and course list not checked). I could not confirm playlist names, so browse the channel for perspective, environment and vehicle videos.
resources.notes: Browse the channel for perspective, vehicle and environment videos and follow one design from thumbnail to polished sketch. Playlist names not confirmed.

resources.title: The Gnomon Workshop: How to Draw Cars (Scott Robertson)
resources.free_notes: Page opened: a 2-hour, 9-lesson workshop. Lessons 1 and 2 (Introduction and Looking at Drawings) are free; lessons 3 to 9 need a Gnomon subscription (price not shown). Scott Robertson's book 'How to Draw' (Design Studio Press) is also paid. I found no verified free official Scott Robertson channel.
resources.notes: Watch the free lessons 1 and 2 (Introduction, Looking at Drawings) for Robertson's approach; lessons 3 to 9 need a subscription. Optional.

practice.title: Wheel ellipses
practice.description: Draw ten wheels in perspective at different angles, each with the correct ellipse and axle line.

practice.title: Car as volumes
practice.description: Draw five cars as a main box, a cabin shape and wheel arches before adding detail.

practice.title: Silhouette thumbnails
practice.description: Thumbnail ten different vehicle silhouettes (car, boat, aircraft, rover, hover vehicle) and pick two.

practice.title: Aircraft cross-section
practice.description: Draw three aircraft with a side silhouette and two cross-sections to place wings and tail.

practice.title: Robot from primitives
practice.description: Draw four robots from cylinders, boxes and spheres, with joints that can plausibly bend.

practice.title: Panel line pass
practice.description: Add panel lines to one finished vehicle, making each line follow the surface's curve.

done_when: Wheels in your drawings share a believable axle and ellipse shape
Your car sketches start with big volumes, not outlines
You can design three distinct vehicle silhouettes in a session
A robot you draw can plausibly move at its joints
Panel lines curve with the body
common_mistakes: Drawing wheels as circles instead of ellipses
Putting panel lines on flat as if the surface were a sheet of paper
Mismatched perspective between front and rear of the same vehicle
Rushing to detail before the body volume is right

school_reference.institution: Petersen Automotive Museum with ArtCenter College of Design
school_reference.note: Free three-module online course; the drawing module is taught by an ArtCenter professor. ArtCenter's own transportation design syllabus was not checked.

title: Architecture: buildings in perspective, roofs, doors and windows, arches, interiors
summary: Buildings are boxes in perspective with roofs, openings and repeated parts. You learn to draw roof types, windows and doors that shrink correctly, arches in perspective, and simple interiors, using sketchers who draw buildings on location and measured drawings from the US survey.
learning_outcomes: Draw a building as a box in one-point or two-point perspective
Name and draw common roof shapes (gable, hip, mansard, gambrel and others)
Place windows and doors that shrink toward the vanishing point
Draw semicircular and pointed arches in perspective
Sketch a simple interior with furniture

resources.title: Liz Steel: Sketching Architecture (blog section)
resources.free_notes: Page opened: nine lessons listed, none marked paid, members-only or login-gated. The page also promotes her paid SketchingNow courses, a Patreon community and in-person workshops.
resources.notes: The page lists nine lessons in this order: Sketching Architecture Essentials, Perspective, Architectural Styles, Architectural Elements and Details, Sketching Architecture Techniques, Interiors, Sketching Architecture Inspiration, Palladio, Architecture Design Sketching. Work through the first six, drawing a building after each, and treat the last three as optional depth.

resources.title: Citizen Sketcher (Marc Taro Holmes): free videos, step-by-step demos and workshop PDFs
resources.free_notes: Downloads page opened: seven free PDFs, including 'Making Expressive Pen and Ink Drawings on Location' (11 pages, made with the Virginia Center for Architecture for an architect audience), 'The Broken Silhouette', 'Drawing People in Motion' and 'Actors on Stage'. None covers perspective. A Free Videos category also exists. His online classes page (citizensketcher.com/videos/) is not marked free; his books and downloadable video classes elsewhere are paid.
resources.notes: Download 'Making Expressive Pen and Ink Drawings on Location' (11-page booklet made with an architecture centre) and do its exercises on a local building; use the other PDFs and free videos for loose watercolour and people. No perspective PDF is listed, so pair it with the Liz Steel Perspective lesson.

resources.title: Library of Congress: HABS/HAER/HALS measured drawings and photographs
resources.provider: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
resources.credit: Historic American Buildings Survey / Historic American Engineering Record, Library of Congress
resources.free_notes: Free to browse online: more than 581,000 measured drawings, large-format photographs and histories for over 43,000 US structures and sites. The page has a 'Rights And Restrictions' section I could not read, so check it before reusing images.
resources.notes: Search for a building type near you and download a measured drawing sheet. Redraw an elevation to learn proportions, then try a section or plan.

resources.title: Urban Sketchers: Learning page (past symposium lectures and workshops)
resources.credit: Urban Sketchers and the individual teachers
resources.free_notes: Page lists symposium lecture videos (for example Richard Briggs, 'Drawing a Sense of Place = Design Tool') and instructor-led workshops, including 'City Perspectives with Nina Johansson' (2022). It does not say whether workshops cost money; the official YouTube channel is public.
resources.notes: Look at the 'City Perspectives with Nina Johansson' workshop and the symposium lecture list for talks on perspective and urban space.

practice.title: Roof shape sheet
practice.description: Draw eight roof types (flat, gable, hip, mansard, gambrel, shed, pyramid, dome) on simple boxes.

practice.title: Row of windows
practice.description: Draw a row of six windows on a wall in two-point perspective so they shrink evenly.

practice.title: Arches in perspective
practice.description: Draw semicircular and pointed arches on a wall at an angle, using ellipse halves.

practice.title: Door and thickness
practice.description: Draw three doors showing the wall depth, frame and step.

practice.title: Interior corner
practice.description: Draw a one-point room with a table, chair and window.

practice.title: Elevation redraw
practice.description: Pick a measured drawing from HABS and redraw one elevation at half size.

done_when: A building you draw uses consistent vanishing points
Windows and doors shrink correctly toward the vanishing point
You can name and draw five roof types from memory
An arch drawn at an angle looks like an arch, not a flat shape
You can draw a room with furniture that sits on the floor
common_mistakes: Using inconsistent vanishing points for different parts of one building
Drawing windows equal width across a receding wall
Leaving out wall thickness around openings
Starting with facade detail instead of the overall box

title: Streets, cities and urban clutter
summary: A street scene needs massing, depth layers and the small clutter that makes a place feel real: signs, poles, bins, cars, people for scale. You practise on-location sketches and thumbnails, and learn to simplify a busy scene into a few big shapes.
learning_outcomes: Simplify a busy street into three to five large masses
Build depth with foreground, middle and background layers
Draw urban clutter (poles, signs, bins, bollards) at the right scale
Use cars and people as scale cues
Finish a 15-minute on-location street sketch

resources.title: Liz Steel: Start urban sketching, urban sketching mindsets, improve your urban sketching
resources.free_notes: Opened: a long blog article (about 23 minutes reading time) with no paywall. It promotes her paid Foundations course (free introductory lessons are offered); related articles linked are Urban sketching mindsets and How to Improve Your Urban Sketching.
resources.notes: Read in this order: How to start urban sketching (about 23 minutes), Urban sketching mindsets, How to Improve Your Urban Sketching. Then use the free introductory lessons of her Foundations course if they appeal, and do the practice below on your own street.

resources.title: Citizen Sketcher (Marc Taro Holmes): free videos, step-by-step demos and workshop PDFs
resources.free_notes: Downloads page opened: seven free PDFs, including 'Making Expressive Pen and Ink Drawings on Location' (11 pages, made with the Virginia Center for Architecture for an architect audience), 'The Broken Silhouette', 'Drawing People in Motion' and 'Actors on Stage'. None covers perspective. A Free Videos category also exists. His online classes page (citizensketcher.com/videos/) is not marked free; his books and downloadable video classes elsewhere are paid.
resources.notes: Use the 'Free Videos', 'Sketching Tips and Tricks' and #OneWeek100People pages for loose scenes and people in places. Not all pages opened.

resources.title: Urban Sketchers official YouTube channel
resources.free_notes: Public YouTube channel with workshop, symposium and sketchcrawl videos. I could not see a playlist list.
resources.notes: Look for chapter sketchcrawl and symposium videos and choose two to see how others edit a busy scene.

resources.title: Library of Congress HABS/HAER/HALS (for street-facing buildings and landscapes)
resources.provider: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
resources.credit: Historic American Buildings Survey / Historic American Engineering Record, Library of Congress
resources.free_notes: Free to browse online: more than 581,000 measured drawings, large-format photographs and histories for over 43,000 US structures and sites. The page has a 'Rights And Restrictions' section I could not read, so check it before reusing images.
resources.notes: Use survey photos of historic streetscapes to study facade rhythm and street furniture, then draw them.

practice.title: Block massing
practice.description: Reduce five street photos to three to five boxes each, with a horizon line.

practice.title: Clutter inventory
practice.description: Draw fifteen pieces of street furniture (poles, bins, signs, bollards, bike racks) at the same scale.

practice.title: Depth layers
practice.description: Draw one street in three layers, with different detail and value for each.

practice.title: Laneway thumbnails
practice.description: Thumbnail six views of a narrow lane or alley, choosing the composition with the strongest depth.

practice.title: Scale cues
practice.description: Add cars and people to two street scenes at the right scale relative to the buildings.

practice.title: On-location sketch
practice.description: Do a single 15-minute street sketch from a bench, without erasing.

done_when: You can simplify a busy street into a few large shapes in under five minutes
Your street scenes have clear depth layers
Street furniture is at believable scale
You finish a 15-minute on-location sketch without giving up
common_mistakes: Trying to draw every sign and window
Giving cars and people inconsistent scale
Leaving no foreground, so the scene looks flat
Correcting endlessly instead of finishing

title: Food and organic still life
summary: Fruit, vegetables, bread and other food make gentle practice in form and light: round volumes, soft edges, reflected light and varied surface texture. You draw single objects, groups and arrangements from life, and study how earlier painters composed still lifes.
learning_outcomes: Draw a fruit or vegetable as a form with light and shadow
Show different surfaces (shiny, matte, rough, wet) in tone
Arrange three objects with overlap and varied sizes
Study how historic still lifes were composed

resources.title: John Muir Laws: gourd and pumpkin studies, mushrooms (plants page)
resources.free_notes: Page metadata describes these as free online tutorials and no paywall appeared. The downloadable flower and leaf model set links to a store-style /product/ page whose price I could not see; the site also sells books and runs paid classes.
resources.notes: From the plants page, do 'Join me down at the Pumpkin Patch' (gourd study for round objects), 'Drawing Pumpkins' and 'Learn to Draw Mushrooms with a Fungi'. I found no verified free food-specific course; these nature-journal lessons transfer well.

resources.title: Rijksmuseum online collection (high-resolution downloads, Dutch still life and design)
resources.free_notes: Page says all freely available works can be downloaded in high resolution for personal and commercial use. It does not name CC0 on that page.
resources.notes: Search the online collection for still-life paintings and prints and study the composition. Free to download in high resolution.

resources.title: The Met Open Access (492,000+ works, CC0)
resources.free_notes: Met states public-domain images and data are CC0, over 492,000 works, flagged with an OA icon in the online collection.
resources.notes: Search for still-life paintings and prints under CC0, and for tableware and vessels to include in your arrangements.

resources.title: Alphonso Dunn: pen and ink, urban sketching and landscape tutorials (YouTube)
resources.free_notes: Channel describes free drawing tutorials. His books and any courses are paid. The page summary mentioned playlists on trees, landscapes, perspective and architecture, but I could not confirm exact playlist names, so search the channel.
resources.notes: Check the channel for pen-and-ink or pencil lessons on fruit or other objects. I could not confirm a food-specific video.

practice.title: Single fruit studies
practice.description: Draw five fruits or vegetables from life, each with a clear light side, shadow side and cast shadow.

practice.title: Surface swap
practice.description: Draw a shiny apple, a matte lemon and a rough potato, changing your marks for each.

practice.title: Three-object group
practice.description: Arrange three objects with overlap and size variety and draw them in 30 minutes.

practice.title: Cut open
practice.description: Draw a cut fruit or vegetable showing its internal structure.

practice.title: Master composition study
practice.description: Pick a Dutch still life, make a thumbnail of its composition and a quick tonal map.

done_when: Each food item you draw looks like a solid form with consistent light
Shiny and matte surfaces read differently
A three-object arrangement shows overlap and clear focal point
You can describe how a historic still life directs the eye
common_mistakes: Outlining everything with the same line weight
Ignoring cast shadows so objects float
Making every object the same size and spacing
Over-rendering one object and leaving others blank

title: Patterns, ornament and surface detail
summary: Pattern work builds a vocabulary of repeating marks and ornamental forms that you can use to decorate objects, clothing, architecture and creatures. You study historical ornament, natural pattern, and structured pattern methods, and learn to wrap pattern around a form.
learning_outcomes: Draw repeat patterns (grids, stripes, scales, spirals) with even spacing
Make ornament from natural forms and from historical sources
Wrap a pattern around a cylinder or sphere using contour lines
Vary scale and density to avoid flat repetition

resources.title: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament (1856), full scan
resources.provider: Internet Archive (Getty Research Institute scan) / Heidelberg University Library
resources.free_notes: Internet Archive item opened: Getty Research Institute scan with online reader, PDF (about 30 MB), EPUB and full text; metadata field says NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, no specific licence named. A second digitisation at Heidelberg University Library (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/diglit/jones1856) returned an access-denied bot page to me. Jones died in 1874.
resources.notes: Open the Internet Archive reader (or download the PDF), flip to three plates from different historical cultures, note what shapes repeat in each, then draw your own pattern in the same spirit. Metadata marks the scan NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

resources.title: Ernst Haeckel, Kunstformen der Natur (Art Forms in Nature, 1899-1904, 100 plates)
resources.free_notes: Scan links come from the Wikipedia article for the work (BHL item 182319, Internet Archive KunstformenderN00Haec, a BHL Flickr album). I did not open each. Haeckel died in 1919, so the plates are old enough to be public domain in most countries.
resources.notes: Choose three plates showing natural symmetry (radial, spiral, branching) and redraw each as a flat decorative pattern.

resources.title: Zentangle: official site, blog and YouTube channel (pattern-by-pattern drawing method)
resources.free_notes: Site lists a YouTube channel, blog, FAQ and glossary as free. Kits, books, teacher training and live workshops are paid or priced.
resources.notes: Free YouTube channel and blog show pattern building one stroke at a time. Skip the paid kits and teacher training.

resources.title: The Met Open Access: textiles, ceramics and decorative arts
resources.free_notes: Met states public-domain images and data are CC0, over 492,000 works, flagged with an OA icon in the online collection.
resources.notes: Search for textiles, wallpaper and ceramics under CC0 and use them as sources for pattern studies.

practice.title: Pattern grid
practice.description: Fill a 4x4 grid with sixteen simple repeat patterns, each in a 2 cm square.

practice.title: Plate-inspired pattern
practice.description: Pick one plate from the Grammar of Ornament and design a new pattern using three of its shapes.

practice.title: Wrap around a form
practice.description: Draw a cylinder and a sphere and wrap a pattern around each, using contour lines.

practice.title: Nature to pattern
practice.description: Take a leaf or shell and turn it into a repeat pattern.

practice.title: Scale and density
practice.description: Draw one pattern at three scales and three densities to see how the feel changes.

done_when: Repeat patterns you draw have even spacing and clear rhythm
A pattern drawn on a form follows the surface
You can create a new design from a historical plate without copying it
You can vary density to guide the eye
common_mistakes: Drawing repeats at uneven spacing, so the rhythm breaks
Laying pattern flat on a curved object
Copying plates stroke for stroke without learning the rule behind them
Using the same scale for all elements
